metadata.title: The Prompt Is The Deliverable.
metadata.subtitle: The Playground Skill (Claude Plugins)
metadata.purpose: Take apart Claude's playground skill: explain how six templates across four zones share the same five-part contract, how a single state object with an updateAll function keeps preview and prompt in sync, and why nothing in the skill actually stops a value-dump output. Land the carry-out that the playground's real output is a prompt, not a list of settings, and that a value dump is a failure, not a variant.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. You'd expect a settings panel to hand you back its settings — border-radius: 8px, shadow-blur: 4, that kind of dump. Playground doesn't. It hands you back a prompt written in English, ready to paste into Claude. So what's the design choice that made a settings panel refuse to output settings?

beats.narration_text: Here's how the skill is organized. Six templates across four zones. Design work — layouts, spacing, color, typography — uses design-playground. Data and queries — SQL, APIs, pipelines, regex — use data-explorer. Learning uses concept-map for knowledge gaps and scope. Review gets three of its own: document-critique, diff-review, and code-map. Different subjects, same shape. And whatever the template, every playground has to meet the same five requirements: one self-contained HTML file with everything inlined, a live preview that updates on every change with no Apply button, a prompt written in natural language instead of a dump of values, a copy button, and three to five presets so the thing looks right the moment it loads. They optimized for one artifact you can email — no server, no build step, no dependencies — at the expense of forcing every template to inline its own tooling.

beats.narration_text: Here's the invariant the whole thing runs on: a single state object. Every control writes to it. Every part of the preview reads from it. And one function — updateAll — refreshes both the preview and the prompt together. Skip that, and it doesn't fail loudly. Read a control's value straight from the page instead of from state, and the live preview quietly stops being reliable. The prompt has its own rule stacked on top: it has to read like an instruction, not a printout. Not 'border-radius: 8px, shadow-blur: 4' — 'a tight border radius with a subtle shadow.' Only the settings that changed from default, with enough context to act on even without the playground open. They optimized for one source of truth at the expense of any shortcut around it. Every control routes through state, or the whole design breaks quietly.

And here's the honest limit. Nothing in the skill actually stops the value-dump output. Whether the generated prompt reads as a natural instruction or as a colon-separated list of settings is left entirely to whoever writes the code — there is no check built in. They chose flexibility over enforcement: the skill teaches the pattern and trusts the coder to follow it. That's why opening the finished file in a browser is a required last step, not an afterthought — the browser is the enforcement layer the skill refused to build. It's the only place a value-dump prompt actually shows itself, before the file ships.
Here's the carry-out. The playground's real output is a prompt, not a list of settings. If what it hands back can't be pasted straight into Claude and acted on, it isn't finished — it's a value dump.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to build an interactive playground skill for Claude Code — a single HTML file the user opens in a browser, tweaks controls in, and copies a generated prompt from. Design it around one invariant: a single state object that every control writes to and every part of the preview reads from, with one updateAll function refreshing preview and prompt together. Walk through it for a design-playground template — a card component with border-radius, shadow, padding, and color. Show the state schema, the control-to-state wiring, the live-preview render function that reads only from state, the prompt-generation function that emits natural-language instructions like 'a tight border radius with a subtle shadow' instead of a colon-separated dump of values and only includes settings that changed from default, three to five presets loaded on startup, and a copy button. Deliver the whole thing as one self-contained HTML file with no external dependencies. Go deeper: ask the same model where a naive implementation quietly breaks — reading a slider's value straight off the DOM instead of from state, forgetting to run updateAll on preset load, or letting the prompt emit every field regardless of whether it changed — and design a lightweight check the coder can run in the browser to catch a value-dump prompt before shipping.
